1009.title: pranayama sequences
1009.hook: a recipe card says where, how long and how many; one short sutra measures the breath the same way
1009.howItsDone: Some teachers of pranayama shape a sequence with the measures of Yoga Sutra 2.50, adjusting where the breath is felt, how long each part lasts and how many rounds are taken.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pranayama sequences at the pace of a keeper taming a lion: gentle first, the hard parts later: little by little. What did you do one step at a time? Day one thousand nine.

A grandmother's recipe card, stained at one corner. It doesn't say much. Which pot. How long on the flame. How many cardamom pods. Three measures, and somehow the whole dish is in them. Change any one, and you get a different dish. Patanjali's Yoga Sutras are written like that card. Each line is short enough to memorize, and it leaves the explaining to the teacher. One of those lines, in the second chapter, measures the breath. And it uses three measures that a cook would recognize. Today, those three, and what they give a sequence.
screen: `A RECIPE CARD.` → `WHICH POT, HOW LONG, HOW MANY.` → `A SUTRA MEASURES THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: Yoga Sutras, chapter two, sutra fifty, in paraphrase. Pranayama has three movements: the breath going out, the breath coming in, and the breath held still. Each is observed by place, by time and by number. And then the breath becomes long and subtle. Take the three measures one at a time. Place, in Sanskrit desha. Commentators read it as where the breath is felt or reaches: the nostrils, the chest, the belly, or how far out the breath goes. Time, kala: how long each movement lasts, which is what counting a slow breath measures. Number, sankhya: how many breaths, how many rounds. Three measures, the way the recipe card had three. Here's what makes this useful for a sequence. A sequence can change any one of the three and keep the other two steady. Keep the place and the number the same, and lengthen only the time. Or keep the time the same and add a few rounds. That's the slow taming from yesterday, given handles you can actually hold. Now notice the goal the sutra names. Not long breaths for their own sake. Long and subtle. The Sanskrit word for subtle, sukshma, means fine, delicate, hard to see. A breath can be long and still rough, like pulling a heavy door. The sutra wants it long and fine, like thread pulled through a needle. So the measures are not the point. They're how a teacher and a student watch the breath closely enough that it can become quiet. In this reading, a good sequence is one where the counting slowly matters less, as the breath grows too fine to measure roughly.
screen: `OUT, IN, HELD STILL.` · `PLACE, TIME, NUMBER.` · `CHANGE ONE MEASURE AT A TIME.` · `THE GOAL: LONG AND SUBTLE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Start with place: where do you feel the breath most right now, the nose, the chest, the belly? Rest your attention there. Now time: count the in-breath and the out-breath, and let them be equal. Keep the place. Then number: decide on a small number of rounds, say six, and count them on your fingers. Keep place and number steady and let only the time stretch, one count longer on the in-breath and one on the out-breath. When the rounds are done, let go of all three, and see if the breath is a little finer than when you began. The bell holds the time.
Pranayama sequences. Breath practices set in an order. Today, the three measures a sequence can move: place, time and number, toward a breath long and subtle.
Your line: place, time, number. Today, once, notice just one of the three: where the breath is, how long it is, or how many you take in a minute. Day one thousand nine.

options: everything: longer, more rounds and a new place, all at once.

1010.title: pranayama sequences
1010.hook: an Upanishad sets its breath advice beside pebbles, sand and the sound of water
1010.howItsDone: Some Hindus who keep a daily breath practice begin by choosing a clean, quiet spot and settling the body upright, following the order the Shvetashvatara Upanishad sets out before the breath itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pranayama sequences measured three ways: place, time, number, toward a breath long and subtle. Which of the three did you catch yourself noticing? Day one thousand ten.

Level ground. No pebbles. No fire nearby. No sand. Somewhere pleasant to the ear, with the sound of water. Out of the wind. It's a checklist a camper would understand, and it sits in one of the Upanishads, right beside its advice on the breath. It sounds almost too practical for a scripture. But the place, the body, the breath and the mind all turn up together in a few short verses. Today, what surrounds the first breath of a sequence.
screen: `LEVEL GROUND, NO PEBBLES.` → `OUT OF THE WIND.` → `RIGHT BESIDE THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: The text is the Shvetashvatara Upanishad, chapter two. Here it is, in paraphrase, in its own order. First the body. Hold it steady, with chest, neck and head upright, and let the senses, together with the mind, settle into the heart. Then the breath. Having restrained the breath, and with movements calmed, breathe out gently through the nostrils. Then the mind. Hold it the way a charioteer holds a chariot yoked to restless horses. Then, in the next verse, the place: level and clean, free of pebbles, fire and sand, pleasant with the sound of water, easy on the eye, sheltered from the wind. Look at what that gives a sequence. It isn't only a chain of breathing techniques. It begins before any of them. Where are you sitting? Is the body upright and steady? Only then does the breath have somewhere to settle. Notice also the word gently. The Upanishad doesn't say breathe out hard, or hold as long as you can. It says out through the nostrils, gently. The strength in this picture belongs to the charioteer's hands, not to the breath. And the horses are restless. The text expects that. It doesn't scold the horses. It asks for a steady driver. That image may be familiar from another Upanishad, the Katha, where the body is a chariot and the senses are horses. Here the same picture shows up in the middle of breath practice. It's close to Patanjali's frame from earlier this week, the seat before the breath, but the Upanishad adds the ground under the seat. So a full sequence, in one reading of these verses, has an order: place, body, breath, mind. Skip the first two, and the breath is being asked to do work the ground and the spine were supposed to do.
screen: `THE BODY: CHEST, NECK, HEAD UPRIGHT.` · `THE BREATH: OUT GENTLY, THROUGH THE NOSE.` · `THE MIND: A CHARIOTEER WITH RESTLESS HORSES.` · `THE PLACE: LEVEL, QUIET, OUT OF THE WIND.`

segments.voice: Before anything else, look at where you are. If there's something you can move, a bag, a cup, a buzzing phone, move it. Then the body: let the chest, neck and head stack upright, without stiffening. Then the breath: a few slow breaths, and let each out-breath leave gently through the nose. Then the mind: when it pulls away like a restless horse, bring it back with a light hand, no scolding. Stay with the gentle out-breath. The bell holds the time.
Pranayama sequences. Breath practices set in an order. Today, the frame the Upanishad gives around them: place, body, breath, mind.
Your line: place, body, breath, mind. Today, before one thing that needs your focus, clear one small pebble from the ground first: a tab, a noise, a mess on the desk. Day one thousand ten.

1011.title: pranayama sequences
1011.hook: after all the lengthening and pausing, the Gita's breath lands somewhere plain: even
1011.howItsDone: Some Hindus who practice pranayama close with a few rounds of even breathing, in and out of equal length, a practice teachers connect with Gita 5.27, where the in-breath and out-breath are made even.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pranayama sequences in the Upanishad's order: place, body, breath, mind. What pebble did you clear before something that needed you? Day one thousand eleven.

A set of old brass scales in a spice shop. The shopkeeper drops a weight on one pan and pours cumin into the other, and for a moment both pans swing. Then they slow. Then they hang level, and the needle in the middle points straight up. That's the moment the sale is made. Nothing dramatic. Just even. Over the past few days the breath has been offered, tamed, measured and given a place to sit. All of it has been about changing the breath in some way. The Gita, in its fifth chapter, has a line about where breath practice settles, and it's as plain as those scales. Today, the last day of pranayama sequences, and the landing.
screen: `TWO PANS OF A SCALE.` → `THEY SWING, THEN HANG LEVEL.` → `WHERE DOES THE BREATH SETTLE?`

segments.voice: Bhagavad Gita, chapter five, verses twenty-seven and twenty-eight, in paraphrase. Shutting out the outside world, with the gaze resting between the brows, making the in-breath and the out-breath even as they move within the nostrils, with the senses, mind and understanding held in check, the sage set on freedom, free of desire, fear and anger, is free indeed. Look at the breath in the middle of that. Not held for a long time. Not forced out. Even. The in-breath and the out-breath are made equal, the two pans of the scale hanging level. The Sanskrit word is sama, even, the same. It shows up elsewhere in the Gita too: being even in pleasure and pain, even toward friend and foe. Here, it reaches all the way down to the breath. Notice also what sits around it. The verse doesn't end at the nostrils. It goes on to desire, fear and anger falling away. The breath is near the center of the line, but the line is about a person. In this picture, an even breath and an even mind travel together. That gives a sequence a direction. The slow counts, the pauses, the measured rounds of this week can all swing the breath one way or another, the way pouring cumin swings the scale. But the Gita's verse points toward where they come to rest: in and out the same. Then nothing more to adjust. This block began with the breath as the power the others rise with, then the seat before the breath, then the breath as an offering, tamed like a lion, measured three ways, set on clean ground. It ends here, level. And tomorrow a new block begins: a mantra, kept day after day, laid on that even breath.
screen: `IN-BREATH AND OUT-BREATH MADE EVEN.` · `SAMA: EVEN, THE SAME.` · `AN EVEN BREATH, AN EVEN MIND.` · `WHERE THE SEQUENCE COMES TO REST.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, place and body settled. For a few rounds, let the breath swing a little: a slightly longer out-breath, then a slightly longer in-breath, like the pans of the scale moving. Then let them meet. In for four, out for four. Breath moving quietly within the nostrils. Keep it even, without strain, round after round. When it's steady, stop counting and see if it stays level on its own. If it tips, even it out again, lightly. The bell holds the time.
Pranayama sequences. Breath practices set in an order. Today, where the Gita lets them settle: in-breath and out-breath made even, like scales hanging level.
Your line: the breath made even. Today, once when you feel tipped, by a message, a delay, a raised voice, take three breaths with the in and the out the same length. Day one thousand eleven.

1012.title: mantra sadhana (a 40-day japa discipline)
1012.hook: Arjuna says holding the mind still is like holding the wind; Krishna doesn't disagree
1012.howItsDone: Hindus who undertake a mantra sadhana may begin with a sankalpa, a resolve naming the mantra, the time, the place and the span, and then keep the practice daily, sometimes with a teacher's guidance.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed pranayama sequences: in-breath and out-breath made even, like scales hanging level: the breath made even. When something tipped you, did you even out the breath? Day one thousand twelve.

The mind is restless, Arjuna says. Turbulent, strong, stubborn. Trying to hold it still, he tells Krishna, seems as hard as holding the wind. It's the sixth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, and Krishna has just described a yogi sitting in perfect steadiness, like a lamp in a windless place. Arjuna's answer is blunt: that sounds lovely, and I can't see how it could last. What's striking is Krishna's reply. He doesn't tell Arjuna he's wrong. He agrees. And then he names the two things that work anyway. Today, a new block begins, and it starts with that reply.
screen: `THE MIND IS LIKE THE WIND.` → `KRISHNA AGREES.` → `THEN HE NAMES WHAT WORKS.`

segments.voice: Gita chapter six, verse thirty-five, in paraphrase: without doubt the mind is restless and hard to hold, but it can be held by practice and by letting go. The word for practice there is abhyasa, steady repeated effort. The word for letting go is vairagya, loosening the grip of wanting. Hold on to the first one. Repeated effort, again and again. That's the ground this new block stands on. Its name has two words. Mantra: a sacred sound or phrase, a syllable like Om, a name of God, a line from a text. Sadhana: a practice kept as a discipline, something done regularly with a purpose. Put them together and mantra sadhana means a mantra kept as a discipline, not said once when the mood is right, but returned to on purpose. The block's title adds japa, which means repetition, and a span, forty days. Tradition gives spans like that; the verses we'll read don't fix a number, and the coming days will look at that. Where does a sadhana begin? In some lineages, with a sankalpa, a resolve, said or held at the start. It sets the terms before the effort starts: which mantra, at what time, where, how long. A sankalpa isn't a mood. It's closer to a promise with the details written in. Here's why that matters, given Arjuna's wind. A restless mind is very good at renegotiating. Shall we do it later? Shorter today? A different mantra? The sankalpa settles those questions once, at the start, so the mind has less to argue with each morning. Krishna's answer was practice. The sankalpa is how practice gets a shape.
screen: `HELD BY PRACTICE AND LETTING GO.` · `MANTRA: A SACRED SOUND OR PHRASE.` · `SADHANA: A PRACTICE KEPT AS DISCIPLINE.` · `SANKALPA: SET THE TERMS AT THE START.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, the way the pranayama days ended: place, body, a few gentle breaths. Then, without saying any mantra yet, set the terms of a small sadhana, just for these coming days. If you pray, you might choose a mantra from your own tradition. If not, Om, or a single word that matters to you, will do. Choose a time of day. Choose a place. Choose a length, small enough to keep. Hold those four things in mind, clearly, like writing them on a card. Then let them go, and sit with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline, returned to on purpose. It begins with practice, abhyasa, and in some lineages with a sankalpa that sets the terms.
Your line: practice, and a resolve. Today, write the four terms down somewhere you'll see them tomorrow: which mantra, what time, where, how long. Day one thousand twelve.

1013.title: mantra sadhana (a 40-day japa discipline)
1013.hook: a string of beads in a coat pocket, one bead larger than the rest, and a rule about never crossing it
1013.howItsDone: Hindus who keep japa may count on a mala, a string of beads of tulsi wood, rudraksha or other materials, moving one bead per repetition and turning the string at the larger meru bead rather than crossing it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mantra sadhana began with Arjuna's wind and Krishna's answer: practice, and a resolve that sets the terms. Did you write your four terms down? Day one thousand thirteen.

In a coat pocket, a loop of beads. Small wooden ones, or knobbly dark seeds, worn smooth by a thumb. One bead is larger than the others and sits apart, with a tassel hanging from it. Some who keep japa follow a rule about that big bead. You go all the way round the loop, bead by bead, and when you arrive back at it, you don't step over it. You turn the whole string around and go back the way you came. Why would a bead be something you don't cross? Today, the mala: the string of beads that goes with japa for some who keep it, and what it's doing in the hand.
screen: `A LOOP OF BEADS IN A POCKET.` → `ONE BEAD SITS APART.` → `YOU DON'T CROSS IT.`

segments.voice: The string is called a mala. The word means a garland, the kind of string of flowers placed around a neck or on an image of God. A japa mala is a garland for counting. The beads vary by tradition. Tulsi wood is tied to devotion to Vishnu and Krishna. Rudraksha seeds, the knobbly dark ones, are tied to Shiva. The large bead is called the meru, the same name as the sacred mountain at the center of the world in Hindu cosmology. Teachers in several lineages say not to cross it, and the reasons they give vary. Some say the meru stands for the guru, or for God, and you don't step over what you honor. Others say turning back keeps the round from becoming mindless, a loop you could spin forever without noticing. Either way, the meru marks a boundary: a round has an end, and you know when you've reached it. Now look at the thread. In the Gita, chapter seven, Krishna says that all of this world is strung on him, like gems on a thread. The beads are what you see. The thread holding them together is hidden. Some who keep japa hold that verse in mind as the beads pass: each repetition separate, all of them strung on one thing. And then there's the thumb. In the Gita's sixth chapter, Krishna says that wherever the restless mind wanders, bring it back. A bead is a small, physical way of doing that. The mind drifts to a bill, a text message, a song. The thumb moves to the next bead. The bead is the coming back, made into something you can feel.
screen: `MALA: A GARLAND FOR COUNTING.` · `THE MERU: THE BEAD YOU DON'T CROSS.` · `GEMS STRUNG ON ONE THREAD.` · `EACH BEAD IS A COMING BACK.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. If you have a mala, hold it. If not, use your fingers: touch the thumb to each fingertip in turn. With each touch, say your mantra once, silently or in a whisper. Om will do, or a word from your own tradition. When the mind drifts, don't scold it. Just let the next touch be the coming back. When you reach the end of a round, pause, turn around, and go back the other way. The bell holds the time.
Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline. Today, the tool in the hand: the mala, its meru, and each bead as a small return.
Your line: each bead a coming back. Today, once when your mind drifts in a queue or on a walk, press your thumb to a fingertip and count it as a bead: one coming back. Day one thousand thirteen.

1014.title: mantra sadhana (a 40-day japa discipline)
1014.hook: who gets to hand you a mantra? the tradition gives more than one answer, and keeps them all
1014.howItsDone: In some Hindu lineages a mantra is received privately from a guru at diksha, initiation; in others, such as the public chanting of the divine names, the mantra is open to anyone who wants to say it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mantra sadhana in the hand: the mala, the meru you don't cross, each bead a coming back. Did your thumb catch a drifting mind? Day one thousand fourteen.

Who gets to hand you a mantra? It sounds like a simple question. In one family, a grandfather leans close to a teenager's ear at a ceremony and whispers a line meant for that ear alone, never to be said aloud to friends. In a park across town, a group sits in a circle singing names of God loud enough for joggers to hear, and anyone who wants to sit down is welcome to join in. Both are mantra. Both are japa, in a way. And both have scripture behind them. Today, how a mantra is chosen, and why the tradition keeps more than one answer.
screen: `A LINE WHISPERED INTO ONE EAR.` → `NAMES SUNG IN A PARK.` → `BOTH HAVE SCRIPTURE BEHIND THEM.`

segments.voice: Start with the whisper. In some lineages, a mantra is received from a guru at diksha, initiation. The teacher chooses it, gives it, and the student keeps it private. The idea is that a mantra given this way carries the teacher's blessing and the lineage's line of practice behind it. In those lineages, picking a mantra off a website isn't the same thing at all. Now the park. There's a short text called the Kali-Santarana Upanishad. In it, the sage Narada asks the god Brahma how to get through the hard age the tradition calls the Kali Yuga. Brahma answers with a mantra made of the names Hare, Rama and Krishna. Narada then asks the obvious follow-up: what are the rules for it? And Brahma says there are no rules. Say it, and that's enough. Some communities point to that line for their open, public chanting of the divine names. Then there's Om. In the Katha Upanishad, Death himself teaches a boy named Nachiketa, and says that the word all the Vedas point to, the word sought by those who live in discipline, is Om. And there are mantras drawn from the old texts, like Om namah shivaya, honoring Shiva, whose words namah shivaya appear in the Shri Rudram. So how does someone choose? The tradition's honest answer is: it depends on the path. A devotee of Krishna, a devotee of Shiva, a student of Vedanta and a beginner with no teacher may each be guided differently. What these answers share is that the mantra comes from somewhere. It isn't invented on the spot. And whichever one is chosen, the sadhana is to stay with it.
screen: `DIKSHA: A MANTRA GIVEN BY A GURU.` · `NARADA ASKS THE RULES: THERE ARE NONE.` · `OM: THE WORD THE VEDAS POINT TO.` · `THE MANTRA COMES FROM SOMEWHERE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, place and body settled. Bring to mind the mantra you chose two days ago, or Om if you haven't chosen. Before saying it, notice where it came from: a teacher, a family, a text, a temple, a song. Let that be part of it. Then begin the japa, silently or in a whisper, one repetition per breath or per bead. If another mantra drifts in, let it pass, and come back to the one you chose. Staying with one is the practice. The bell holds the time.
Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline. Today, where the mantra comes from: a guru's diksha, the open names, or the word the Vedas point to.
Your line: where the mantra comes from. Today, find out one thing about where your chosen mantra comes from: its text, its tradition, or who first gave it to you. Day one thousand fourteen.

1015.title: mantra sadhana (a 40-day japa discipline)
1015.hook: dawn and dusk are the hinges of the day; an old law book hangs the mantra on both
1015.howItsDone: Some Hindu families keep sandhya, a rite at dawn and dusk built around the Gayatri, and some who keep a mantra sadhana tie it to those same hinges of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mantra sadhana and where the mantra comes from: a guru's diksha, the open names, the word the Vedas point to. What did you learn about the source of yours? Day one thousand fifteen.

Just before sunrise, the street is gray. No color yet, no shadows. A man stands on a rooftop facing east, lips moving, and he doesn't sit down. He's waiting for something. Then the first edge of the sun clears the water tank on the next building, and he stops. That evening, on the same roof, he sits facing west and keeps going until the first star shows. He isn't watching a clock. He's watching the sky. It looks like a personal habit. It has a text behind it. Today, the time a mantra is kept, and why one text ties it to the edges of the light.
screen: `A ROOFTOP BEFORE SUNRISE.` → `STANDING UNTIL THE SUN SHOWS.` → `SITTING UNTIL THE FIRST STAR.`

segments.voice: The text is the Manusmriti, the Laws of Manu, one of the old books of dharma, in its second chapter. In paraphrase: at the morning twilight, one should stand, repeating the Savitri, the verse also known as the Gayatri, until the sun is seen. At the evening twilight, one should sit, repeating it until the stars appear. Look at how the timing works. There's no hour in it. The edges are set by the sky: the sun's first appearance in the morning, the stars at night. The practice fills the in-between. The word for these joints of the day is sandhya, a joining, the place where night meets day and day meets night. The daily rite kept at those times is called sandhya too, and in some families it's still kept that way, at dawn and dusk, with this verse at its heart. You don't need that rite to see what the timing gives a sadhana. A mantra hung on a hinge of the day doesn't need a reminder. The light changes, and the mantra comes with it. This is what the last week has been building. Pranayama sequences gave the breath an order and the stillness after. Then the mantra sadhana: Krishna's answer to the restless mind, practice; a sankalpa to set the terms; the mala in the hand, each bead a coming back; and where the mantra comes from. Today adds the when. Not when it's convenient. When the day turns. Morning or evening, whichever one you can keep. A practice tied to a hinge, some teachers say, is easier to keep than one waiting for a free moment, because free moments rarely arrive on their own.
screen: `STAND AT DAWN UNTIL THE SUN SHOWS.` · `SIT AT DUSK UNTIL THE STARS APPEAR.` · `SANDHYA: THE JOINING OF THE DAY.` · `HANG THE MANTRA ON A HINGE.`

segments.voice: Wherever you are in the day right now, notice the light. Is it morning, afternoon, evening? Sit comfortably, place and body settled, a few gentle breaths. Then begin your mantra, silently or in a whisper, and let it run. As you do, choose your hinge: the first light, or the last. Decide that tomorrow the mantra starts there, when the light changes, not when a free moment turns up. Then keep going with the mantra until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline. Today, its when: hung on the hinges of the day, dawn and dusk, the sandhya.
Your line: dawn and dusk. Today, at dusk, look for the moment the light changes, and say your mantra once, right then. Day one thousand fifteen.
